narrative:
The model predicted a 60.6% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three pieces of information about your academic record. Your class ranking at the end of your third year was the strongest factor and pushed the prediction toward failure. You placed in the second decile, noticeably lower than the average ranking of accepted students. Your first-year ranking was the third most important factor and also worked against you, again landing in the second decile while accepted students averaged around the sixth.

Surprisingly, your LSAT score worked in the opposite direction. At 42 it is higher than the average of accepted applicants (37), so this result pulled the prediction toward passing. However, the two weaker class rankings outweighed the positive LSAT signal, resulting in an overall outlook of likely failure.

You should focus on strengthening your academic performance and class standing. Consider retaking key courses, seeking additional academic support, or gaining targeted work experience that demonstrates your ability to succeed in law school before reapplying. Improving your upper-year performance will have the biggest impact on future predictions. (218 words)
